title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 48 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 368–371 (Night 48, continuing directly from nights-47), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 48 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Prince Sharkān follows the Christian girl into a marble-gated palace and a monastery hall of fountains and gilded couches, where he is fed and left to spend a sleepless night of regret, reciting verse. At dawn the girl returns in splendour among her attendants, names him as Sharkān son of ʿUmar, swears by the Messiah that he is safe under her protection, eats from the dishes herself to dispel his fear of poison, and plies him with wine until he loses his senses. The night breaks off as Shahrazad perceives the morning. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-arbaʿūn
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the forty,
sentences.i: And when it was the forty-eighth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ النَّصْرَانِيَّةَ لَمَّا قَالَتْ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ لِشَرْكَانَ وَهُوَ يَسْمَعُهُ وَأَنَّهُ إِنْ وَقَعَ شَرْكَانُ فِي يَدِي فَإِنِّي أَخْرُجُ لَهُ فِي صِفَةِ الرِّجَالِ وَأَجْعَلُهُ فِى الْقُيُودِ وَالْأَ غْلَالِ بَعْدَأَنْ أَسَرَهُ مِنْ بَدْرِ سَرْجِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ṣabiyyata al-naṣrāniyyata lammā qālat hādhā al-kalāma li-Sharkāna wa-huwa yasmaʿuhu wa-annahu in waqaʿa Sharkānu fī yadī fa-innī akhruju lahu fī ṣifati al-rijāli wa-ajʿaluhu fī al-quyūdi wa-al-aghlāli baʿda an asarahu min badri sarjihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king, the happy, that the Christian girl, when she said this speech to Sharkān, and he was hearing it, and that if Sharkān fell into my hand, then I would go out to him in the form of men, and put him in the fetters and the shackles, after [I] seized him from the moon of his saddle.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the Christian girl said these words in Sharkān's hearing, while he listened, she said that if Sharkān fell into her hands, she would go out to him in the guise of a man and put him in fetters and shackles, once she had taken him captive from his saddle.
sentences.n: The sentence begins with a that-clause (أَنَّ … لَمَّا قَالَتْ) and then slides into the girl's own words, with "my hand" and "I will go out", before it ever finishes; that is ordinary Middle Arabic storytelling, so read the second half as her direct speech. The verb in بَعْدَأَنْ أَسَرَهُ is printed as a bare third-person form, though the speaker is "I"; we point it as printed (أَسَرَهُ, "seized him") and translate "after I seized him". بَعْدَأَنْ is printed as one word. الْأَ غْلَالِ is printed with a space after the alif, as the edition has it (read al-aghlāl, "the shackles"). بَدْرِ سَرْجِهِ, literally "the full moon of his saddle", is obscure; it may mean the rider who sits resplendent in his saddle, so "from his saddle" is a reading, not a certainty.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ شَرْكَانُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ أَخَذَتْهُ النَّخْوَةُ وَالْحَمِيَّةُ وَغَيْرَةُ الْأَ بْطَالِ وَأَرَادَأَنْ يُظْهِرَ لَهَا نَفْسَهُ وَيَبْطِشَ بِهَا وَلَكِنْ رَدَّهُ عَنْهَا جَمَالُهَا فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ —
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Sharkānu hādhā al-kalāma akhadhat-hu al-nakhwatu wa-al-ḥamiyyatu wa-ghayratu al-abṭāli wa-arāda an yuẓhira lahā nafsahu wa-yabṭisha bihā wa-lākin radda-hu ʿanhā jamāluhā fa-anshada yaqūlu —
sentences.l: And when Sharkān heard this speech, there took him the pride and the zeal and the jealousy-of the heroes, and he wanted that he show to her himself and lay hold on her; but her beauty turned him back from her; and he recited, saying —
sentences.i: When Sharkān heard these words, pride and fierce zeal seized him, and the jealous honour of a warrior; he longed to reveal himself to her and to fall upon her. But her beauty held him back from her, and he recited, saying —
sentences.n: أَخَذَتْهُ النَّخْوَةُ is the Arabic way of saying a feeling "takes" a man: the verb comes first and agrees with the feminine noun that follows it. بَطَشَ بِهِ is "to seize violently, to set upon". أَرَادَأَنْ is printed as one word. The "—" at the end is in the print and marks the coming poem; الْأَ بْطَالِ has a space after the alif, as printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا الْمَلِيحُ اَتَى بِذَنْبٍ وَاحِدِ * جَاءَتْ مَحَاسِنُهُ بِأَلْفِ شَفِيحِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā al-malīḥu atā bi-dhanbin wāḥidin * jāʾat maḥāsinuhu bi-alfi shafīḥin
sentences.l: And when the handsome one comes with one offence * his beauties come with a thousand intercessors.
sentences.i: When a lovely one commits a single fault, his charms come to plead for him by the thousand.
sentences.n: The verse is copied as the edition prints it. The last word is printed شَفِيحٍ with a ḥāʾ; the sense demands شَفِيع (shafīʿ), "intercessor", which is the word the next poem takes up with شَافِع, so this is surely a misprint, but it is kept as printed. اَتَى is printed with a bare alif carrying a fatḥa, for أَتَى "comes".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَعِدَتْ وَهُوَ فِي أَثَرِهَا فَنَظَرَ شَرْكَانُ إِلَى ظَهْرِ الْجَارِيَةِ فَرَأَى أَرْدَافَهَا تَتَلَاطَمُ كَالْأَ مْوَاجِ فِى الْبَحْرِ الرَّجْرَاجِ فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣaʿidat wa-huwa fī atharihā fa-naẓara Sharkānu ilā ẓahri al-jāriyati fa-raʾā ardāfahā tatalāṭamu ka-al-amwāji fī al-baḥri al-rajrāji fa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then she went up, and he in her track; and Sharkān looked at the back of the girl, and saw her buttocks dashing against one another like the waves in the quaking sea; and he recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: Then she went up, with him following in her footsteps. Sharkān looked at the girl's back and saw her buttocks surging against one another like waves upon a heaving sea, and he recited these verses.
sentences.n: أَرْدَاف (sing. رِدْف) are the hips and buttocks; تَتَلَاطَمُ is the word for waves dashing against each other, and the poet's image is the same. كَالْأَ مْوَاجِ has a space after the alif in the print, kept as printed (read ka-al-amwāj).

sentences.t:
فِي وَجْهِهَا شَافِعٌ يَمْحُو إِسَاءَتَهَا * مِنَ الْقُلُوبِ وَجِيهٌ حَيْثُمَا شَفَعَا
اِذَا تَأَمَّلْتُهَا نَادَيْتُ مِنْ عَجَبٍ * اَلْبَدْرُ فِي لَيْلَةِ الْاِكْمَالِ قَدْ طَلَعَا
لَوْ اَنَّ عِفْرِيتَ بِلْقِيسٍ يُصَارِعُهَا * مَعْ وَصْفِ قُوَّتِهِ فِي سَاعَةٍ صُرِعَا
sentences.tr:
fī wajhihā shāfiʿun yamḥū isāʾatahā * mina al-qulūbi wajīhun ḥaythumā shafaʿā
idhā taʾammaltuhā nādaytu min ʿajabin * al-badru fī laylati al-ikmāli qad ṭalaʿā
law anna ʿifrīta Bilqīsa yuṣāriʿuhā * maʿ waṣfi quwwatihi fī sāʿatin ṣuriʿā
sentences.l:
In her face is an intercessor, who wipes out her ill-doing * from the hearts, a man of standing wherever he intercedes.
When I gaze at her I cry out in wonder: * The full moon, on the night of completion, has risen!
If the ʿifrīt of Bilqīs wrestled her * for all the description of his strength, in an hour he would be thrown down.
sentences.i: In her face is an advocate who wipes her faults from every heart, an advocate of honour wherever he pleads. When I gaze at her I cry out in wonder, "The moon has risen on the night of its fullness!" And if Bilqīs's own ʿifrīt were to wrestle her, for all that is told of his strength, within the hour he would be thrown.
sentences.n: The verse is copied as the edition prints it, vowel marks and all, including the bare alif with kasra or fatḥa in اِذَا, اَلْبَدْرُ, الْاِكْمَالِ and اَنَّ. The "intercessor" is her face's beauty, which pleads for her as in the first poem. لَيْلَةُ الْإِكْمَالِ is the night of the full moon, when the moon is complete. The ʿifrīt of Bilqīs recalls the strong jinn of the Solomon-and-Sheba story; here it only stands for the mightiest champion imaginable, and the point is the girl's strength, which matches the wrestling to come.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالَا سَائِرِينَ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَا إِلَى بَابٍ مُقَنْطَرٍ وَكَانَتْ قَنْطَرَتُهُ مِنْ رُخَامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālā sāʾirīna ilā an waṣalā ilā bābin muqanṭarin wa-kānat qanṭaratuhu min rukhāmin
sentences.l: And the two did not cease going on until the two arrived at a gate, arched, and its arch was of marble.
sentences.i: On and on they went, until they came to an arched gate whose arch was of marble.
sentences.n: The dual يَزَالَا and وَصَلَا are the prince and the girl. مُقَنْطَر is "arched, vaulted", from قَنْطَرَة, "arch".

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الْبَابَ وَدَخَلَتْ وَمَعَهَا شَرْكَانُ وَسَارَا إِلَى دِهْلِيزٍ طَوِيلٍ مُقَبًّى عَلَى عَشْرِ قَنَاطِرَ مَعْقُودَةٍ وَعَلَى كُلِّ قَنْطَرَةٍ قِنْدِيلٌ مِنَ الْبِلَّوْرِ يَشْتَعِلُ كَشُعَاعِ النَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥati al-jāriyatu al-bāba wa-dakhalat wa-maʿahā Sharkānu wa-sārā ilā dihlīzin ṭawīlin muqabban ʿalā ʿashri qanāṭira maʿqūdatin wa-ʿalā kulli qanṭaratin qindīlun mina al-billawri yashtaʿilu ka-shuʿāʿi al-nāri
sentences.l: And the girl opened the gate and entered, and with her Sharkān, and the two went to a corridor, long, vaulted upon ten arches, bound, and upon every arch a lamp of crystal, kindling like the ray of fire.
sentences.i: The girl opened the gate and went in, with Sharkān beside her, and the two came into a long vaulted passage that stood on ten bound arches; from every arch hung a crystal lamp that blazed like a ray of fire.
sentences.n: مُقَبًّى is a passive participle spelled with a final ى, "vaulted". مَعْقُودَة is literally "tied, knotted", the architect's word for an arch whose stones are bound into a curve. After عَشْر "ten" the counted noun is a genitive plural, عَشْرِ قَنَاطِرَ "ten arches".

sentences.t: فَتَلَقَّتْهَا الْجَوَارِي فِي آخِرِا لِلْ هِلِيزِ بِالشُّمُوعِ الْمُطَيَّبَةِ وَعَلَى رُؤُسِهِنَّ الْعَصَائِبُ الْمُزَرْكَشَةُ بِالْفُصُوصِ الَّتِي هِيَ مِنْ سَائِرِ أَصْنَافِ الْجَوَاهِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-talaqqathā al-jawārī fī ākhirā lil hilīzi bi-al-shumūʿi al-muṭayyabati wa-ʿalā ruʾūsihinna al-ʿaṣāʾibu al-muzarkashatu bi-al-fuṣūṣi allatī hiya min sāʾiri aṣnāfi al-jawāhiri
sentences.l: And the maidens met her in the end of the corridor with the candles, the perfumed, and upon their heads the headbands, the embroidered with gems, which are of all kinds of jewels.
sentences.i: At the far end of the passage maidens met her bearing scented candles, and on their heads they wore headbands worked with gems of every kind of jewel.
sentences.n: The edition prints آخرا لل هليز, three pieces, where the sense plainly wants "at the end of the corridor" (آخِرِ الدِّهْلِيزِ). We keep the printed letters and point them as printed; the stray alif and the broken word are the edition's. الْجَوَارِي is the plural of جَارِيَة, "girl, slave-girl". مُزَرْكَشَة, "embroidered, inlaid", is a Persian-derived word.

sentences.t: وَسَارَتْ وَهُنَّ أَمَامَهَا وَشَرْكَانُ وَرَاءَهَا إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى الدَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-sārat wa-hunna amāmahā wa-Sharkānu warāʾahā ilā an waṣalū ilā al-dayri
sentences.l: And she went, and they before her, and Sharkān behind her, until they arrived at the monastery.
sentences.i: She walked on with the maidens before her and Sharkān behind, until they reached the monastery.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ بِدَائِرِ ذَلِكَ الدَّيْرِ أَسِرَّةً مُقَابِلَةً لِبَعْضِهَا وَعَلَيْهَا سُتُورٌ مُكَلَّلَةٌ بِالذَّهَبِ وَأَرْضُ الدَّيْرِ مَفْرُوشَةٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ الرُّخَامِ الْمُجَزَّعِ وَفِي وَسَطِهِ بِرْكَةُ مَاءٍ عَلَيْهَا أَرْبَعَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ فَوَّارَةً مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْمَاءُ يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا كَاللُّجَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada bi-dāʾiri dhālika al-dayri asirratan muqābilatan li-baʿḍihā wa-ʿalayhā sutūrun mukallalatun bi-al-dhahabi wa-arḍu al-dayri mafrūshatun bi-anwāʿi al-rukhāmi al-mujazzaʿi wa-fī wasaṭihi birkatu māʾin ʿalayhā arbaʿatun wa-ʿishrūna fawwāratan mina al-dhahabi wa-al-māʾu yakhruju minhā ka-al-lujayni
sentences.l: And he found at the circuit of that monastery beds facing one another, and upon them curtains, crowned with gold; and the floor of the monastery spread with kinds of marble, the veined; and in the middle of it a pool of water, upon it four and twenty fountains of gold, and the water coming out from them like silver-liquid.
sentences.i: All around that monastery he found beds set facing one another, with curtains over them wrought with gold. The floor was spread with veined marbles of every kind, and in the midst of it lay a pool of water crowned with twenty-four golden fountains, and the water poured from them like liquid silver.
sentences.n: أَسِرَّةً takes a nunation fatḥa as the object of وَجَدَ. The edition itself prints the shadda on اسرّة. In "four and twenty" the units come first and the counted noun after, in the accusative (فَوَّارَةً). اللُّجَيْن, "silver" (a poetic word), is the simile for the flowing water.

sentences.t: وَرَأَى فِى الصَّدْرِ سَرِيرًا مَفْرُوشًا بِالْحَرِيرِ الْمَلُوكِيِّ
sentences.tr: wa-raʾā fī al-ṣadri sarīran mafrūshan bi-al-ḥarīri al-malūkiyyi
sentences.l: And he saw, in the upper part, a couch spread with silk, the royal.
sentences.i: At the head of the hall he saw a couch spread with royal silk.
sentences.n: الصَّدْر is the "breast", hence the place of honour, the upper end of a hall. الْمَلُوكِيّ is the printed form of "royal" (Classical مَلَكِيّ).

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْجَارِيَةُ اصْعَدْ يَامَوْلَائِي عَلَى هَذَا السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-jāriyatu iṣʿad yāmawlāʾī ʿalā hādhā al-sarīri
sentences.l: And the girl said to him: Go up, O my master, upon this couch.
sentences.i: Then the girl said to him, "Go up, my lord, onto this couch."
sentences.n: يَامَوْلَائِي is printed as one word, with a hamza-seat ئ where Classical has مَوْلَايَ; we point what the text says.

sentences.t: فَصَعِدَ شَرْكَانُ فَوْقَ السَّرِيرِ وَذَهَبَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَغَابَتْ سَاعَةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣaʿida Sharkānu fawqa al-sarīri wa-dhahabati al-jāriyatu wa-ghābat sāʿatan mina al-zamāni
sentences.l: And Sharkān went up above the couch, and the girl went, and was absent an hour of the time.
sentences.i: Sharkān climbed onto the couch, and the girl went away and was gone for an hour.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَ عَنْهَا مِنْ بَعْضِ الْخُدَّامِ فَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّهَا ذَهَبَتْ إِلَى مَرْقَدِهَا وَنَحْنُ نَخْدُمُكَ كَمَا أَمَرْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala ʿanhā min baʿḍi al-khuddāmi fa-qālū lahu innahā dhahabat ilā marqadihā wa-naḥnu nakhdumuka kamā amarta
sentences.l: And he asked about her of some of the servants, and they said to him: She has gone to her place-of-lying, and we serve you as you commanded.
sentences.i: He asked some of the servants about her, and they told him, "She has gone to her bed, and we are here to wait on you as you command."
sentences.n: مِنْ بَعْضِ is partitive, "some of". We read كَمَا أَمَرْتَ as active, "as you commanded", though a passive "as you were commanded" is also possible from the bare letters.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ قَدَّمُوا لَهُ مِنْ غَرَائِبِ الْأَلْوَانِ فَأَكَلَ حَتَّى اكْتَفَى
sentences.tr: thumma innahum qaddamū lahu min gharāʾibi al-alwāni fa-akala ḥattā iktafā
sentences.l: Then they presented to him of the rarities of the colours, and he ate until he was sufficed.
sentences.i: Then they set before him rare dishes of every kind, and he ate until he had had his fill.
sentences.n: أَلْوَان, "colours", is the idiom for "kinds", here kinds of food.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ قَدَّمُوالَهُ طَشْتًا مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَإِبْرِيقًا مِنَ الْفِضَّةِ فَغَسَلَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum qaddamūlahu ṭashtan mina al-dhahabi wa-ibrīqan mina al-fiḍḍati fa-ghasala yadayhi
sentences.l: Then they presented-to-him a basin of gold and a ewer of silver, and he washed his hands.
sentences.i: Then they brought him a golden basin and a silver ewer, and he washed his hands.
sentences.n: قَدَّمُوالَهُ is printed as one word, verb and لَهُ run together. The basin and ewer are for washing the hands after the meal.

sentences.t: وَخَاطِرُهُ عِنْدَ عَسْكَرِهِ لِكَوْنِهِ لَايَعْلَمُ مَاجَرَى لَهُمْ بَعْدَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-khāṭiruhu ʿinda ʿaskarihi li-kawnihi lāyaʿlamu mājarā lahum baʿdahu
sentences.l: And his mind was with his army, because of his not-knowing what had happened to them after him,
sentences.i: Yet his heart was with his army, for he did not know what had befallen them after he left.
sentences.n: The edition runs لَا يَعْلَمُ and مَا جَرَى together as single words (lāyaʿlamu, mājarā); they are kept as printed. خَاطِر is the "mind, heart", what passes through one's thoughts. لِكَوْنِهِ is li- plus the verbal noun "his being", so "because he did not know".

sentences.t: وَيَتَذَكَّرُ أَيْضًا كَيْفَ نَسِيَ وَصِيَّةَ أَبِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-yatadhakkaru ayḍan kayfa nasiya waṣiyyata abīhi
sentences.l: and he was remembering also how he forgot the testament of his father,
sentences.i: and he remembered, too, how he had forgotten his father's charge,
sentences.n: The وَصِيَّة is the counsel Sharkān's father, King ʿUmar, gave him before he set out.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ مُتَحَيِّرًا فِي أَمْرِهِ نَادِمًا عَلَى مَا فَعَلَ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُوَبَانَ النَّهَارُ فَتَنَهَّدَ وَتَحَسَّرَ عَلَى مَافَعَلَ وَصَارَ غَرِيقًا فِي بِحَارِ الْفِكْرِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra mutaḥayyiran fī amrihi nādiman ʿalā mā faʿala ilā an ṭalaʿa al-fajruwabāna al-nahāru fa-tanahhada wa-taḥassara ʿalā māfaʿala wa-ṣāra gharīqan fī biḥāri al-fikri wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: and he became bewildered in his affair, remorseful over what he had done, until the dawn rose-and-appeared the day; and he sighed and lamented over what-he-did, and became drowned in the seas of thought, and recited, saying:
sentences.i: so that he fell into bewilderment about his plight, bitterly regretting what he had done, until dawn rose and the day appeared. Then he sighed and grieved over his deed, drowned in seas of thought, and he recited:
sentences.n: The edition prints الفجروبان as one word, "the dawn and appeared", with the conjunction run on; it is kept as printed, as are مافعل and the other run-together words. مُتَحَيِّرًا and نَادِمًا are accusative states describing him.

sentences.t:
لَمْ اَعْلِمِ الْحَزْمَ وَلْكِنَّنِي * دُهِيتْ فِي الْاَمْرِ فَمَا حِيلَتِي
لَوْ كَانَ مَنْ يَكْشِفُ عَنِّي الْهَوى * بَرِئْتُ مِنْ حَوْلِي وَمِنْ قُوَّتِي
وَاِنَّ قَلْبِي فِي ضَلَالِ الْهَوى * صَبٌّ وَاَرْجُو اللَّهَ فِي شِدَّتِي
sentences.tr:
lam aʿlimi al-ḥazma wa-lkinnanī * duhītu fī al-amri fa-mā ḥīlatī
law kāna man yakshifu ʿannī al-hawā * bariʾtu min ḥawlī wa-min quwwatī
wa-inna qalbī fī ḍalāli al-hawā * ṣabbun wa-arjū Allāha fī shiddatī
sentences.l:
I did not know prudence, but I * was struck down in the affair, so what is my device?
If there were one who would uncover from me the passion * I would be quit of my might and of my strength.
And truly my heart, in the straying of passion, * is love-smitten, and I hope for God in my distress.
sentences.i: I knew no prudence, but disaster has struck me in this matter, and what remedy have I? If there were one who could lift this passion from me, I would give up all my might and strength. My heart is lost in the wanderings of love, sick with longing, and in my distress I hope in God.
sentences.n: The verse is copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all. In the first line اَعْلِمِ is printed with a kasra on the mīm, which would be the jussive linking to the article; we read it as "I did not know" (lam aʿlam). دُهِيتْ is the passive "I was struck by a calamity"; the printed sukūn on the tā is kept. In the second line the apodosis بَرِئْتُ مِنْ means "I would be rid of, I would disown", a way of saying he would gladly give up his strength to be freed. صَبٌّ is "one smitten with love".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَإِذَا بِبَهْجَةٍ عَظِيمَةٍ قَدْ أَقْبَلَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi wa-idhā bi-bahjatin ʿaẓīmatin qad aqbalat
sentences.l: And when he was finished with his poetry — and behold, with a great splendour, it had approached.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, behold, a great splendour came toward him.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِبَهْجَةٍ is the "and behold" construction: the bi- only marks what appears. The sentence has no main verb after lammā; the narrative simply turns to what he sees next.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ فَإِذَا هُوَ بِأَكْثَرَ مِنْ عِشْرِينَ جَارِيَةً كَالْأَقْمَارِ حَوْلَ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَهِيَ بَيْنَهُنَّ كَالْبَدْرِ بَيْنَ الْكَوَاكِبِ يَحْجُبْنَ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara fa-idhā huwa bi-akthara min ʿishrīna jāriyatan ka-al-aqmāri ḥawla tilka al-jāriyati wa-hiya baynahunna ka-al-badri bayna al-kawākibi yaḥjubna tilka al-jāriyata
sentences.l: And he looked, and behold, it was with more than twenty girls, like the moons, around that girl, and she among them like the full moon among the stars, they screening that girl.
sentences.i: He looked, and there were more than twenty girls, bright as moons, around that young woman, and she in their midst like the full moon among the stars, as they screened her from view.
sentences.n: فَإِذَا هُوَ بِـ is another "behold" form: bi- marks what he suddenly sees. "That girl" (تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةُ) is the Christian girl who led Sharkān in, now returned among her attendants in rich dress; the word جَارِيَة simply means "girl, maid, young woman". يَحْجُبْنَ is a feminine plural verb with a circumstantial sense.

sentences.t: وَعَلَيْهَا دِيبَاجٌ مُلُوكِيٌّ وَقَدْ شَدَّتْ فِي وَسَطِهَا زُنَّارًا مَحْبُوكًا مُرَصَّعًا بِأَ نْوَاعِ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَقَدْ ضَمَرَ خَصْرُهَا وَأُبْرِزَ رِدْفَاهَا فَصَارَتَا كَأنَّهُمَا كَثِيبَ بَلُّورٍ تَحْتَ قَضِيبٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَنَهْدَاهَا كِفْلَيْنِ مِنَ الرُّمَّانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿalayhā dībājun mulūkiyyun wa-qad shaddat fī wasaṭihā zunnāran maḥbūkan muraṣṣaʿan bi-a nawāʿi al-jawāhiri wa-qad ḍamara khaṣruhā wa-ubriza ridfāhā fa-ṣāratā kaʾannahumā kathība ballūrin taḥta qaḍībin min fiḍḍatin wa-nahdāhā kiflayni mina al-rummāni
sentences.l: And upon her was a brocade, royal, and she had girded in her middle a girdle, closely-woven, studded with kinds of jewels; and her waist was slender, and her two buttocks were brought out, and the two became as if they were a dune of crystal beneath a branch of silver; and her two breasts, two portions from the pomegranate.
sentences.i: She wore a royal brocade, and about her waist she had bound a close-woven girdle studded with every kind of jewel. Her waist was slender and her hips stood out full, so that they seemed a dune of crystal beneath a slender rod of silver, and her breasts were like two halves of a pomegranate.
sentences.n: The edition prints بانواع with a stray space, "bi-a nawāʿ"; we keep it and point the two pieces as they stand. وَأُبْرِزَ is read as a passive, "were brought out", since the dual subject رِدْفَاهَا follows it. كِفْلَيْنِ is obscure: كِفْل is a "portion" or "share", and "two portions of pomegranate" suits a rounded breast; the word may be corrupt, so take this as a reading, not a certainty. The dual pronoun is followed by a singular كَثِيبَ, a Middle Arabic looseness.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ شَرْكَانُ ذَلِكَ كَادَ عَقْلُهُ أَنْ يَطِيرَ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ وَنَسِيَ عَسْكَرَهُ وَوَزِيرَهُ وَتَأَمَّلَ رَأْسَهَا فَرَأَى عَلَيْهَا شَبَكَةً مِنَ اللُّؤْلُؤِ مُفَصَّلَةً بِأَنْوَاعِ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَالْجَوَارِي عَنْ يَمِينِهَا وَيَسَارِهَا يَرْفَعْنَ أَذْ يَا لَهَا وَهِيَ تَتَمَايَلُ عُجْبًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara Sharkānu dhālika kāda ʿaqluhu an yaṭīra mina al-faraḥi wa-nasiya ʿaskarahu wa-wazīrahu wa-taʾammala raʾsahā fa-raʾā ʿalayhā shabakatan mina al-luʾluʾi mufaṣṣalatan bi-anwāʿi al-jawāhiri wa-al-jawārī ʿan yamīnihā wa-yasārihā yarfaʿna adh yā lahā wa-hiya tatamāyalu ʿujban
sentences.l: And when Sharkān looked at that, his mind all but flew from joy, and he forgot his army and his vizier; and he contemplated her head and saw upon her a net of pearl, set with kinds of jewels, and the girls at her right and her left lifting her tails, and she swaying in vanity.
sentences.i: When Sharkān saw this, his wits all but flew away for joy, and he forgot his army and his vizier. He gazed at her head and saw upon it a net of pearls set with jewels of every kind, while the maidens on her right and left held up her train as she swayed along in her pride.
sentences.n: كَادَ عَقْلُهُ أَنْ يَطِيرَ is "his mind nearly flew"; kāda here takes أَنْ, which is ordinary Middle Arabic practice. The edition prints اذيالها, "her trains", as three pieces, اذ يا لها; we keep the stray spacing and point each piece. عُجْبًا is read as "vanity, conceit" (a gait of pride), not عَجَبًا "wonder"; both are possible from the unpointed letters.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ وَثَبَ شَرْكَانُ قَائِمًا لَمَّارَأَى حُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا فَصَاحَ زِنْهَارِ زِنْهَارِ مِنْ هَذَا الزُّنَّارِ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika wathaba Sharkānu qāʾiman lammāraʾā ḥusnahā wa-jamālahā fa-ṣāḥa zinhāri zinhāri min hādhā al-zunnāri thumma anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And at that, Sharkān leapt up standing, when he saw her beauty and her loveliness, and he cried, "Zinhār, zinhār, from this girdle!" — then he recited, saying, these verses.
sentences.i: At that Sharkān sprang to his feet, seeing her beauty and her loveliness, and cried out, "Mercy, mercy, from this girdle!" Then he recited these verses.
sentences.n: The edition prints لمارأى as one word, "lammā raʾā"; kept fused. زِنْهَار is a Persian-derived cry meaning "beware" or "quarter, mercy". It puns on الزُّنَّار, the girdle (here also the Christian zunnār belt): his cry is "spare me from this girdle", since the girdle is the lady herself.

sentences.t:
ثَقِيلَةُ الْاَرْدَافِ مَائِلَةٌ * خُرْعُوبَةٌ نَاعِمَةُ النَّهْدِ
تَكَتَّمَتْ مَا عِنْدَهَا مِنْ جَوًى * وَلَسْتُ أَكْتُمُ الَّذِي عِنْدِي
خُدَّ اُمَّهَا يَمْشِينَ مِنْ خَلْفِهَا * كَالْقَيْلِ فِي حَلٍ وَفِي عَقْلِ
sentences.tr:
thaqīlatu al-ardāfi māʾilatun * khurʿūbatun nāʿimatu al-nahdi
takattamat mā ʿindahā min jawan * wa-lastu aktumu alladhī ʿindī
khuddi ummahā yamshīna min khalfihā * ka-al-qayli fī ḥallin wa-fī ʿaqli
sentences.l:
Heavy of the hips, swaying * slender-supple, soft of the breast.
She concealed what is with her of passion * and I do not conceal that which is with me.
A cheek — her mother — they walk behind her * like the chieftain in loosing and in binding.
sentences.i: Heavy-hipped she is, and swaying, slender and supple, soft of breast. She has hidden what she feels of longing, but I will not hide what is in me. Her attendants walk behind her, like a chieftain's court in its loosing and binding.
sentences.n: The verse is copied exactly as the edition prints it, marks and all. The third line is unclear: خُدَّ اُمَّهَا ("cheek … her mother") makes little sense and is probably corrupt; the sense of the line, "they walk behind her", points to something like "her attendants", but that is a guess and we have not altered the print. الْقَيْل is a petty king or chieftain, and "loosing and binding" (حَلٍّ وَعَقْدٍ) is the stock phrase for authority; the print has عقل, "binding" in the sense of hobbling.

sentences.t: فَجَعَلَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ تَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهِ زَمَانًا طَوِيلًا وَتُكَرِّرُ فِيهِ النَّظَرَ إِلَى أَنْ تَحَقَّقَتْهُ وَعَرَفَتْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-jaʿalati al-jāriyatu tanẓuru ilayhi zamānan ṭawīlan wa-tukarriru fīhi al-naẓara ilā an taḥaqqaqat-hu wa-ʿarafat-hu
sentences.l: And the girl set to looking at him for a long time, and repeating upon him the gaze, until she made sure of him and knew him.
sentences.i: The girl went on gazing at him for a long while, studying him again and again, until she was certain of him and knew him.
sentences.n: The girl is the Christian maiden who brought the prince into the monastery. تَحَقَّقَتْهُ is "she verified him": she checked what she had suspected about who he was.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ بَعْدَأَنْ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ قَدْ أَشْرَفَ وَأَضَاءَ بِكَ الْمَكَانُ يَاشَرْكَانُ كَيْفَ كَانَتْ لَيْلَتُكَ يَا هَمَّامُ بَعْدَ مَا مَضَيْنَا وَتَرَكْنَاكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu baʿda an aqbalat ʿalayhi qad ashrafa wa-aḍāʾa bika al-makānu yāSharkānu kayfa kānat laylatuka yā Hammām baʿda mā maḍaynā wa-tarakanāka
sentences.l: And she said to him, after she turned to him: The place has risen-high and shone-bright by you, O Sharkān! How was your night, O high-minded one, after what we went on and left you?
sentences.i: Then she turned to him and said, "Your coming has made the whole place shine, O Sharkān! How did you pass your night, O Hammām, after we went our way and left you?"
sentences.n: The edition prints بعدان ("after that") and ياشركان as single words, and we keep them run together. اشرف is printed; it would most naturally mean "rose high / grew noble", though the pairing with اضاء "shone" makes a slip for اشرق "shone" a real possibility; either way the sense is a compliment, "the place is lit up by you". She greets him as Sharkān and then as يَا هَمَّامُ; هَمَّام is an epithet of praise, "high-minded one", used here as a form of address.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ الْكَذِبَ عِنْدَالْمُلُوكِ مَنْقَصَةٌ وَعَارٌ لَاسِيَّمَا عِنْدَ الْمُلُوكِ الْكِبَارِ وَأَنْتَ شَرْكَانُ بْنُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ فَلَا تَكْتُمْ سِرَّكَ وَحَالَكَ وَلَا تُسْمِعْنِي بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ غَيْرَ الصِّدْقِ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يُورِثُ الْبُغْضَ وَالْعَدَاوَةَ فَقَدْ نَفَذَ فِيكَ سَهْمُ الْقَضَاءِ فَعَلَيْكَ بِالتَّسْلِيمِ وَالرِّضَاءِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lahu inna al-kadhiba ʿinda al-mulūki manqaṣatun wa-ʿārun lā siyyamā ʿinda al-mulūki al-kibāri wa-anta Sharkānu ibnu al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni fa-lā taktum sirraka wa-ḥālaka wa-lā tusmiʿnī baʿda dhālika ghayra al-ṣidqi fa-inna al-kadhiba yūrithu al-bughḍa wa-al-ʿadāwata fa-qad nafadha fīka sahmu al-qaḍāʾi fa-ʿalayka bi-al-taslīmi wa-al-riḍāʾi
sentences.l: Then she said to him: Surely lying, among kings, is a defect and a shame, especially among the great kings; and you are Sharkān, son of the king ʿUmar, son of al-Nuʿmān. So do not hide your secret and your state, and do not let me hear after that other than the truth; for lying brings-on hatred and enmity. For the arrow of decree has pierced in you; so upon you is submission and contentment.
sentences.i: Then she said to him, "Lying is a blemish and a disgrace among kings, above all among great kings; and you are Sharkān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. So hide neither your secret nor your state, and let me hear nothing but the truth from you hereafter, for lying breeds hatred and enmity. The arrow of fate has struck home in you, so yield to it and be content."
sentences.n: عِنْدَالْمُلُوكِ and لاسيما are printed run together and kept so. عَلَيْكَ بِـ is a standing idiom, "you had better hold to …", and the girl uses it to urge him to accept his fate calmly. Note that she addresses him as the son of King ʿUmar: she has known who he was from the moment she recognised him.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَالَتْ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يُمْكِنْهُ النُّكْرَانُ فَصَدَّقَهَا عَلَى ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ أَنَا شَرْكَانُ بْنُ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ الَّذِي عَذَّ بَنِي الزَّمَانُ وَأَوْقَعَنِي فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ فَمَهْمَا شِئْتِ فَا فْعَلِيهِ الْآنَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qālat dhālika lam yumkin-hu al-nukrānu fa-ṣaddaqahā ʿalā dhālika fa-qāla anā Sharkānu ibnu ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni alladhī ʿadhdha banī al-zamānu wa-awqaʿanī fī hādhā al-makāni fa-mahmā shiʾti fā ifʿalī-hi al-āna
sentences.l: And when she said that, denial was not possible to him, so he confirmed her on that, and said: I am Sharkān, son of ʿUmar, son of al-Nuʿmān, he whom time tormented-me and cast me in this place; so whatever you wish, do it now.
sentences.i: When she had spoken so, he could not deny it, and he conceded that she was right. "I am Sharkān, son of ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān," he said, "the man whom Time has tormented and thrown into this place. So do now whatever you wish."
sentences.n: The edition prints عذ بني as two words; it is one, عَذَّبَنِي "tormented me" (the shadda is the edition's own and is kept). Notice the resumptive pronoun: الَّذِي عَذَّبَنِي الزَّمَانُ is literally "who time tormented-me". The last clause is printed فا فعليه; we read it as فَافْعَلِيهِ, "so do it", with the imperative to a woman, which suits the speaker: Sharkān puts himself in the girl's hands. The reading is ours and the print is clearly a little damaged here.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَتْ بِرَأْسِهَا إِلَى الْأَرْضِ زَمَانًا طَوِيلًا ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ طِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّعَيْنًا فَأَنَّكَ ضَيْفِي وَصَارَ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكَ خُبْزٌ وَمِلْحٌ فَأَنْتَ فِي ذِمَّتِي وَفِي عَهْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqat bi-raʾsihā ilā al-arḍi zamānan ṭawīlan thumma iltafatat ilayhi wa-qālat lahu ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan fa-annaka ḍayfī wa-ṣāra baynanā wa-baynaka khubzun wa-milḥun fa-anta fī dhimmatī wa-fī ʿahdī
sentences.l: And she bowed with her head to the ground a long time; then she turned to him and said to him: Be good of soul and cool of eye, for you are my guest, and there has come to be between us and between you bread and salt; so you are in my pledge and in my covenant.
sentences.i: She bowed her head to the ground for a long while; then she turned to him and said, "Take heart and be of good cheer, for you are my guest, and bread and salt now lie between us. You are under my protection and my covenant."
sentences.n: طِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّ عَيْنًا are fixed phrases of comfort: "be good of soul and cool of eye" (a cool eye is a contented one). The edition prints وقرعينا as one word, and the opening of the next clause as فأنك, where we should expect فإنك; we keep the print and read it so. Eating bread and salt together makes a bond of hospitality that protects the guest.

sentences.t: فَكُنْ آمِنًا وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ لَوْأَرَادَ أَهْلُ الْأَرْضِ أَنْ يُؤْذُوكَ لَمَا وَصَلُوا إِلَيْكَ إِلَّا أَنْ خَرَجَتْ رُوحِي مِنْ أَجْلِكَ فَأَنْتَ فِي أَمَانِ الْمَسِيحِ وَأَمَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-kun āminan wa-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi law arāda ahlu al-arḍi an yuʾdhūka la-mā waṣalū ilayka illā an kharajat rūḥī min ajlika fa-anta fī amāni al-Masīḥi wa-amānī
sentences.l: So be secure; and by the right of the Messiah, if the people of the earth wished to harm you, they would not reach you, unless my soul had gone out for your sake; for you are in the safe-conduct of the Messiah and my safe-conduct.
sentences.i: "So be at ease. By the Messiah's right, if all the people of the earth sought to harm you, they could not reach you unless my soul first left my body for your sake; for you are under the Messiah's protection, and mine."
sentences.n: لَمَا here is la-mā, "would not" (the lām that answers لَوْ plus the negative mā), not لَمَّا "when". The edition prints لواراد as one word. Her oath is by the Messiah because she is a Christian.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَتْ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَصَارَتْ تُلَاعِبُهُ إِلَى أَنْ زَالَ مَا عِنْدَهُ مِنَ الْخَوْفِ وَعَلِمَ أَنَّهَا لَوْكَانَ لَهَا أَرَبٌ فِي قَتْلِهِ لَفَعَلَتْهُ مِنَ اللَّيْلَةِ الْمَاضِيَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasat ilā jānibihi wa-ṣārat tulāʿibu-hu ilā an zāla mā ʿindahu mina al-khawfi wa-ʿalima annahā law kāna lahā arabun fī qatlihi la-faʿalat-hu mina al-laylati al-māḍiyati
sentences.l: And she sat down at his side and began toying with him, until what was with him of fear went away, and he knew that, had she had a purpose in killing him, she would have done it from the night just past.
sentences.i: She sat down beside him and went on playing with him until his fear melted away, and he understood that, had she wished him dead, she would have done it the night before.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا كَلَّمَتْ جَارِيَةً بِلِسَانِ الرُّومِيَّةِ فَغَابَتْ سَاعَةً وَأَنَتْ إِلَيْهَا وَمَعَهَا كَأْسٌ وَمَائِدَةُ طَعَامٍ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā kallamat jāriyatan bi-lisāni al-Rūmiyyati fa-ghābat sāʿatan wa-anat ilayhā wa-maʿahā kaʾsun wa-māʾidatu ṭaʿāmin
sentences.l: Then she spoke to a girl in the tongue of the Greek (al-Rūmiyya), and she was absent an hour, and she came to her, and with her a cup and a table of food.
sentences.i: Then she spoke to a maidservant in the Greek tongue and was gone for an hour. The maid returned, bringing a cup and a table laden with food.
sentences.n: The edition prints وانت, which can only be a slip for وأتت "and she came" (compare فاتتها a few lines later, where the same verb is spelled correctly); it is pointed here as the letters stand. The subject of "came" is the maid who was sent off, returning. الرُّومِيَّة is "the Greek (language)", the tongue of the Christian girl.

sentences.t: فَتَوَقَّفَ شَرْكَانُ عَنِ الْأَكْلِ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ رُبَّمَا وَضَعَتْ شَئًا فِي ذَلِكَ الطَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-tawaqqafa Sharkānu ʿani al-akli wa-qāla fī nafsihi rubbamā waḍaʿat shayʾan fī dhālika al-ṭaʿāmi
sentences.l: And Sharkān held back from the eating, and said in his self: Perhaps she has put a thing in that food.
sentences.i: Sharkān held back from eating, and said to himself, "Perhaps she has put something in that food."
sentences.n: شَيْئًا is printed شيا, with no hamza and no seat for it; it is pointed as the ordinary word شَيْئًا "something". رُبَّمَا, "perhaps", is followed by a past verb, which is the normal construction.

sentences.t: فَعَرَفَتْ مَا فِي ضَمِيرِهِ فَالْتَفَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿarafat mā fī ḍamīrihi fa-iltafatat ilayhi wa-qālat lahu
sentences.l: And she knew what was in his inmost mind, and she turned to him, and said to him:
sentences.i: She knew what was in his mind, and turned to him, and said:

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ لَيْسَ الْأَمْرُ كَذَلِكَ وَهَذَا الطَّعَامُ لَيْسَ فِيهِ شَئٌ مِنَ الَّذِي تَتَوَهَّمُهُ وَلَوْ كَانَ خَاطِرِي فِي قَتْلِكَ لَقَتَلْتُكَ فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi laysa al-amru ka-dhālika wa-hādhā al-ṭaʿāmu laysa fīhi shayʾun mina alladhī tatawahhamuhu wa-law kāna khāṭirī fī qatlika la-qataltuka fī hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: "And by the right of the Messiah, the matter is not thus, and this food, there is not in it a thing of that which you imagine; and if my mind had been on your killing, I would have killed you at this very time."
sentences.i: "By the Messiah's right, it is not as you suppose. There is nothing in this food of what you fancy. Had I meant to kill you, I would have killed you this very moment."
sentences.n: وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ is the oath-formula met a few lines above: wa- of oath, with the genitive. Note that she swears by the Messiah, as a Christian would, and the Muslim prince is expected to trust it. لَوْ كَانَ … لَقَتَلْتُكَ is the standard contrary-to-fact pair: a perfect verb after law, la- before the answer. خَاطِرِي, literally "my passing thought", is the mind's inclination.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَى الْمَائِدَةِ وَأَكَلَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ لَوْنٍ لُقْمَةً
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddamat ilā al-māʾidati wa-akalat min kulli lawnin luqmatan
sentences.l: Then she advanced to the table and ate from every colour a morsel.
sentences.i: Then she went forward to the table and ate a morsel from every dish.
sentences.n: لَوْن is "colour", and by extension a kind or variety, hence "every dish".

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَكَلَ شَرْكَانُ فَفَرِحَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَكَلَتْ مَعَهُ إِلَى أَنِ اكْتَفَيَا وَغَسَلَا يَدَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika akala Sharkānu fa-fariḥati al-jāriyatu wa-akalat maʿahu ilā ani iktafayā wa-ghasalā yadayhimā
sentences.l: And at that, Sharkān ate, and the girl rejoiced, and she ate with him until they were satisfied, and they washed their two hands.
sentences.i: Only then did Sharkān eat, and the girl was glad, and she ate with him until both were sated, and they washed their hands.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ أَنْ غَسَلَا أَيْدِيهِمَا قَامَتْ وَأَمَرَتْ جَارِيَةً أَنْ تَأْتِيَ بِالرَّيَاحِينِ وَآلَاتِ الشَّرَابِ مِنْ أَوَانِى الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَالْبِلَّوْرِ وَأَنْ يَكُونَ الشَّرَابُ مِنْ سَائِرِ الْأَلْوَانِ الْمُخْتَلِفَةِ وَالصِّفَاتِ فَأَتَتْهَا بِجَمِيعِ مَا طَلَبَتْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda an ghasalā aydīhimā qāmat wa-amarat jāriyatan an taʾtiya bi-al-rayāḥīni wa-ālāti al-sharābi min awānī al-dhahabi wa-al-fiḍḍati wa-al-billawri wa-an yakūna al-sharābu min sāʾiri al-alwāni al-mukhtalifati wa-al-ṣifāti fa-atathā bi-jamīʿi mā ṭalabathu
sentences.l: And after they washed their hands she arose, and commanded a girl to bring the sweet-herbs and the implements of the drink, of vessels of the gold and the silver and the crystal, and that the drink be of all the varied kinds and qualities; and she brought her all that she had asked.
sentences.i: When they had washed their hands, she rose and ordered a maid to bring fragrant herbs and the implements of drinking, in vessels of gold, silver and crystal, and to have the wine of every sort, in all its varieties and qualities. The maid brought her everything she asked for.
sentences.n: أَمَرَ بِـ is "command (someone) to bring"; here the verb takes أَنْ plus a subjunctive instead, and بِالرَّيَاحِينِ is the thing to be brought: تَأْتِيَ بِـ is "come with", that is, "bring". أَوَانِى is printed with a final ى, the plural of إِنَاء "vessel", pointed as printed. الشَّرَاب is the drink, which in this setting means wine.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ مَلَأَتْ أَوَّلَ قَدَحٍ وَشَرِبَتْهُ قَبْلَهُ كَمَا فَعَلَتْ فِى الطَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata malaʾat awwala qadaḥin wa-sharibathu qablahu ka-mā faʿalat fī al-ṭaʿāmi
sentences.l: Then the girl filled the first cup and drank it before him, as she had done with the food.
sentences.i: Then the girl filled the first cup and drank it before him, just as she had done with the food.
sentences.n: She drinks first, as she ate first, to show the prince the wine is safe. كَمَا فَعَلَتْ is "as she did"; فِى is printed with ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَلَأَتْ ثَانِيًا وَأَعْطَتْهُ إِيَّاهُ فَشَرِبَ
sentences.tr: thumma malaʾat thāniyan wa-aʿṭathu iyyāhu fa-shariba
sentences.l: Then she filled a second, and gave him it, and he drank.
sentences.i: Then she filled a second cup and handed it to him, and he drank.
sentences.n: أَعْطَتْهُ إِيَّاهُ is "she gave him it": the second object is the independent pronoun إِيَّاهُ, as Classical Arabic does when two pronoun objects follow a verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا مُسْلِمُ انْظُرْ كَيْفَ أَنْتَ فِى أَلَّلِ عَيْشٍ وَمَسَرَّةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā Muslimu unẓur kayfa anta fī allali ʿayshin wa-masarratin
sentences.l: And she said to him: O Muslim, look how you are in the [?most delightful] of life and gladness.
sentences.i: Then she said to him, "O Muslim, see how you are in the most delightful life, and in joy."
sentences.n: The edition prints الّل with a shadda on the first lām. It is almost certainly a printer's slip for ألذّ "most delightful", the elative of لَذِيذ, and we translate it so; it is pointed as the letters and the printed shadda stand. يَا مُسْلِمُ is a plain "O Muslim", a title the girl gives him.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَشْرَبُ مَعَهُ وَتَسْقِيهِ إِلَى أَنْ غَابَ عَنْ رُشْدِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tashrabu maʿahu wa-tasqīhi ilā an ghāba ʿan rushdihi
sentences.l: And she did not cease drinking with him and giving him to drink, until he was absent from his right-mindedness.
sentences.i: And she went on drinking with him, and pouring for him, until he lost his wits.
sentences.n: لَمْ تَزَلْ تَشْرَبُ is the "did not cease doing" construction: لَمْ يَزَلْ plus a present verb means "continued to". غَابَ عَنْ رُشْدِهِ, "he was absent from his right-mindedness", is the idiom for being drunk past reason.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Then the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unsaid.
sentences.n: The night breaks off here, and the next begins with the usual formula. The two clauses rhyme (الصَّبَاح / الْمُبَاح, -āḥ). الْكَلَام الْمُبَاح, "the permitted speech", is the stock phrase for the tale she is allowed to tell.
